title: Manage soil fertility and plant nutrition

lessons.title: Plant nutrients and soil fertility
lessons.html:
What is soil fertility?

Soil fertility is the soil's ability to supply plants with the nutrients, water and air they need. It depends on chemical properties (nutrients, pH), physical properties (texture, structure, depth, drainage) and biological properties (organic matter and soil life).

Essential nutrients

GroupNutrientsNotes
Macronutrients (needed in large amounts)Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K)N for leaf and stem growth; P for roots, flowering and energy; K for water regulation, fruit quality and disease resistance
Secondary nutrientsCalcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), Sulphur (S)Ca for cell walls (lack causes blossom-end rot in tomatoes); Mg is part of chlorophyll
Micronutrients (small amounts)Zinc, iron, manganese, boron, copper, molybdenumSmall amounts, but deficiencies can sharply cut yield

Typical deficiency symptoms

  • Nitrogen: yellowing of older, lower leaves first; slow, stunted growth.
  • Phosphorus: purplish leaves, poor root growth, delayed maturity.
  • Potassium: scorched or yellow leaf edges on older leaves.
  • Magnesium: yellowing between veins on older leaves.
  • Iron: yellowing between veins on young leaves.

Symptoms can look similar and can be caused by other problems such as waterlogging, disease or herbicide damage. Confirm with soil and leaf analysis.

Soil pH

pH controls nutrient availability. Many South African soils, especially in high-rainfall areas, are acidic, which can cause aluminium toxicity and reduce availability of P, Ca and Mg. Lime is applied to correct acidity, at rates based on soil analysis. Very alkaline soils can reduce availability of micronutrients like iron and zinc.

Organic matter

Organic matter improves structure, water-holding capacity and nutrient supply and feeds soil organisms. Build it with crop residues, compost, manure, cover crops and reduced tillage.

lessons.title: Soil sampling and fertiliser programmes
lessons.html:
Soil sampling

A fertiliser programme is only as good as the soil sample. Follow the lab's instructions, generally:

  1. Divide the farm into uniform sampling blocks (same soil type, crop and history).
  2. Take many sub-samples in a zigzag pattern across each block with a clean auger at the correct depth for the crop.
  3. Avoid unusual spots: fence lines, kraals, old fertiliser heaps, roads, wet patches.
  4. Mix sub-samples in a clean bucket and fill the lab bag with the required amount.
  5. Label: farm, block, depth, date, crop history and planned crop.

Leaf or tissue analysis, especially in orchards and vineyards, complements soil analysis.

Building a fertiliser programme

An agronomist or fertiliser adviser uses soil results, the yield target, crop needs and previous applications to recommend products, rates and timing. As supervisor, you must implement it accurately.

Types of fertiliser

  • Inorganic: straight (e.g. urea, LAN, superphosphate, potassium chloride) or compound (e.g. N:P:K mixtures).
  • Organic: manure, compost, chicken litter, bone meal; slower release, also add organic matter.
  • Liming materials: calcitic or dolomitic lime.
  • Foliar feeds and fertigation: nutrients through leaves or irrigation water.

Applying correctly: the 4 Rs

  • Right source: the product recommended.
  • Right rate: calibrate spreaders and planters; check the kg per hectare.
  • Right time: e.g. split nitrogen applications to match crop uptake and reduce leaching.
  • Right place: banded, broadcast, side-dressed or fertigated as specified.

Safety and environment

  • Wear gloves, dust masks and eye protection as on the product label.
  • Store fertilisers dry and away from fuel; some are oxidisers and fire risks.
  • Do not apply near watercourses or before heavy rain; run-off causes algae in dams and rivers.
  • Fertilisers are regulated under Act 36 of 1947: use registered products.

Records

Record block, product, rate, date, method and operator. Compare with yields and later soil tests.

Key points

  • N, P and K are the main nutrients; secondary and micronutrients also matter.
  • pH controls nutrient availability; lime corrects acidity.
  • Sample soil correctly and label clearly.
  • Follow the 4 Rs: right source, rate, time and place.
  • Calibrate equipment, protect water and keep records.
